claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu composite consisting of uncoated tungsten particles embedded in a copper matrix.
A nanoscale nickel diffusion interlayer can be deposited onto tungsten particles by electroless plating or a similar technique before composite fabrication.
A thin Ni interlayer improves wettability between tungsten and copper.
A thin Ni interlayer improves adhesion between tungsten and copper.
Improved W–Cu interfacial wettability and adhesion lower interfacial thermal resistance.
The Ni coating improves chemical bonding at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni coating reduces interfacial mismatch that would otherwise scatter conduction electrons.
Reduced electron scattering at the W–Cu interface improves thermal energy transport and raises composite thermal conductivity.
The Ni layer acts as a barrier that limits propagation of irradiation-induced defects across the W–Cu interface.
Limiting irradiation-induced defect propagation preserves the composite's mechanical strength.
Relative to an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite, the Ni-coated composite will have measurably higher thermal conductivity.
The Ni-coated composite will retain mechanical durability essentially comparable to that of an uncoated W–Cu control.
The Ni-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance essentially comparable to that of an uncoated W–Cu control.
Fusion-reactor joint materials experience high temperature, high heat flux, and intense high-energy neutron irradiation.
Standard powder-metallurgy or infiltration methods can be used to fabricate the proposed Ni-coated W–Cu composite.
The predicted benefit requires the Ni coating to remain nanoscale and stable at the operating temperatures and irradiation doses.
Excessively thick Ni coatings could compromise composite performance.
High-temperature-induced interdiffusion involving the Ni layer could compromise composite performance.
Matched Ni-coated and uncoated W–Cu specimens subjected to identical thermal cycling and irradiation provide a controlled test of the hypothesis.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant thermal-conductivity improvement while retaining comparable mechanical and irradiation properties, or degradation of the Ni coating under operating conditions, would falsify the hypothesis.
